source: Fields of Several Charges and Field Lines
Add the field vectors from each charge; field lines show the direction, and their spacing shows the strength.
Students think field lines are the paths charges must follow, or that two lines can cross.
With several charges, each one makes its own field, and the field at a point is their vector sum, for the same reason that forces add. Field lines then let you see the whole pattern at a glance.

The force on a test charge is the vector sum of the forces from each charge. Divide every force by the test charge and the same sum holds for fields: $\vec E = \vec E_1 + \vec E_2 + \cdots$. Field lines are drawn so that at every point they run along $\vec E$, and so that they crowd together where $E$ is strong. Since the field has only one direction at each point, two lines can never cross.

Add the field vectors from each charge. Field lines start on positive charges and end on negative ones, point along $\vec E$, are closer where the field is stronger, and never cross. They show the direction of the force, not the path a charge must follow.
Two equal positive charges: the lines bend apart, and the field is zero at the midpoint.
The same idea as arrows: the field of a positive and a negative charge, drawn on a grid.
Worked examples
A $+2.0\,\text{nC}$ and a $-2.0\,\text{nC}$ charge are $0.20\,\text{m}$ apart. Find the field at the midpoint.
The middle of a dipole
The positive charge's field points away from it, toward the negative charge; the negative charge's field points toward itself. Same direction.
$E = 1798 + 1798 = 3.60 \times 10^{3}\,\text{N/C}$, toward the negative charge.
A $+2.0\,\text{nC}$ charge is at the origin and a $+4.0\,\text{nC}$ charge at $(0.30\,\text{m}, 0.40\,\text{m})$. Find the field at P $= (0.30\,\text{m}, 0)$.
Fields at a right angle
From the origin, $0.30\,\text{m}$ away: $E_1 = (8.99 \times 10^{9})\dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-9}}{(0.30)^2} = 200\,\text{N/C}$, in the $+x$ direction.
From the charge $0.40\,\text{m}$ above P: $E_2 = (8.99 \times 10^{9})\dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{-9}}{(0.40)^2} = 225\,\text{N/C}$, in the $-y$ direction.

Thinking field lines are the paths charges must follow, or that two lines can cross. A field line shows the direction of the force, which sets the direction of the acceleration, not of the velocity; a moving charge can cut across lines, just as a thrown ball does not follow the downward pull of gravity. And lines never cross, because at a crossing the field would have two directions at once.
